title: Meet Dukaan: your first program
intro: In this course you will build one real thing: Dukaan, a shop management system. Today it is a few lines that list stock on a screen. Step by step it will grow — a database, an API, a website, a live deployment, AI features. At the end you will demo a complete system in interviews and prove you can build software from scratch. It all starts here, with lesson 1: a program is instructions plus data.
objectives: Explain what a program is in one sentence: instructions plus data.
Run a Python program and describe what each line does.
Change one value, predict the new output, and check your prediction.

concepts.title: You are building Dukaan
concepts.text: Here is the whole journey, so you always know where you are. Days 1-7: Dukaan is a command-line stock list. Days 8-14: it gets version control and tests. Days 15-21: it gets AI features, like a chatbot that answers stock questions. Days 22-30: it becomes a real API on the internet. Days 31-90: a database, a website, logins, deployment on cloud servers. Each step happens because the shop outgrows the last version — that is how you will learn architecture: by feeling why each piece is needed.

concepts.title: A program is instructions plus data
concepts.text: Data is the facts: the shop name, the item names, the prices. Instructions are what to do with the facts: remember this value, show that line on the screen. Code is just these two things written down. When you run the program, Python reads your instructions from top to bottom and carries them out. Everything you will ever build — websites, APIs, AI systems — is instructions plus data, stacked higher.

concepts.title: Your three tools
concepts.text: You need three tools, and they do three different jobs. The editor (VS Code) is where you write the instructions. Python is the runner — it reads your file and carries out the instructions. The terminal is the messenger — you type 'python dukaan.py' there, which means 'hey computer, run this file with Python.' Never type terminal commands inside your Python file, and never paste Python code into the terminal as a command. Three tools, three jobs.

concepts.title: Predict before you run
concepts.text: Here is the habit that separates engineers from typists: before you run a changed program, say out loud what you expect to see. Then run it. If you were right, you understand it. If you were wrong, you just found something to learn — read the lines in order until you see why. Do this every time, starting today.

example.run: Run python dukaan.py from the starter directory.
example.context: Amina's shop needs a stock list on screen. Three items, three prices. Read the code, predict the exact output, then run it.
example.code:
shop_name = "Amina Store"
item1 = "Rice"
price1 = 250
item2 = "Sugar"
price2 = 180
item3 = "Tea"
price3 = 950

print(f"Welcome to {shop_name}")
print(f"1. {item1} - Rs {price1}")
print(f"2. {item2} - Rs {price2}")
print(f"3. {item3} - Rs {price3}")
example.output:
Welcome to Amina Store
1. Rice - Rs 250
2. Sugar - Rs 180
3. Tea - Rs 950
example.walkthrough: The first seven lines store data: one shop name, three item names, three prices. Text goes inside quotation marks; prices are plain numbers. The last four lines are instructions: print shows text on the screen, and the f before the quotation marks lets the stored values appear inside the text. Python runs top to bottom, so the welcome line prints first. This is Dukaan v0.1 — the seed of everything you will build.

exercises.title: Change the shop
exercises.task: Change the shop name to your own shop name and change one price. First write down exactly what the output will look like. Then run it.
exercises.hint: Only change the values on the right side of the = sign.
exercises.check: The output matches your written prediction exactly.

exercises.title: Add an item
exercises.task: Add a fourth item with its price, and one more print line so it appears in the list.
exercises.hint: Copy the pattern: one line to store the name, one line to store the price, one print line to show it.
exercises.check: Four items print, each with the correct price.

exercises.title: Break it on purpose
exercises.task: Delete one quotation mark and run the program. Read the error message carefully — which line does it blame? Then fix it.
exercises.hint: Python tells you the line number. The real mistake is often just before it.
exercises.check: You can point at the error and explain in your own words what went wrong.

mistakes: Typing 'python dukaan.py' inside the Python file — that is a terminal command, not a Python instruction.
Forgetting quotation marks around text — Python then thinks your words are instruction names.
Changing three things at once when something breaks — change one thing, predict, run, observe.
fde: In a software house, a junior's first tickets look exactly like this: small, clear, testable. 'Show the stock list on screen.' Senior engineers trust juniors who write small programs they can explain line by line. That is what you practiced today — the atom of the job. Every system you will ever build is made of atoms like this one.

project.title: Dukaan v0.1 — the stock list
project.brief: Amina runs a small shop. She keeps stock in her head and on paper slips. She wants a program that shows her stock list on screen: item names and prices, clear enough to read at a glance. Build version 0.1 — it only displays the list. This is the first brick of the system you will grow for the whole course.
deliverables: A dukaan.py file that runs with python dukaan.py and shows the stock list.
The program's output, copied into your notes or a screenshot.
A two-line README: what the program does and how to run it.

milestones.title: Show the shop name
steps: Create dukaan.py in your editor.
Store the shop name and print a welcome line.
Run it from the terminal.
milestones.check: The welcome line prints with your shop name.

milestones.title: List three items
steps: Store three item names and three prices.
Print each item on its own line with its price.
Run it and read the full list.
milestones.check: All three items show with the correct prices.

milestones.title: Change it and predict
steps: Change one price.
Write down what you expect the output to be.
Run it and compare.
milestones.check: Your prediction matches the real output.

acceptance: python dukaan.py runs with no errors.
The shop name appears on the first line.
Three items appear, each with the correct price.
Changing a price changes only that line in the output.
You can explain every line to another person without reading.
tests: Welcome to Amina Store, then 3 items priced 250, 180, 950
The Rice line shows Rs 300; the other lines are unchanged
The first line shows the new shop name
Delete one quotation mark and run
Python shows an error naming the line (then fix it and re-run)
extensions: Ask the shopkeeper: use input() to ask for the shop name when the program starts.
Add a total: print the sum of all three prices as the last line.
review: Can you explain each line without looking at the screen?
Did you predict the output before running, at least twice?
To add a fourth item, what would you change — and how many minutes would it take?

title: Data, variables, types, and conversion
intro: A value's type determines what operations mean. Two values can look identical on a screen and still behave differently inside a program. This lesson connects types to real failures in quantities, user input, and conversion tools. Your project is a conversion desk that accepts values deliberately, checks them, and produces clearly labelled results.
objectives: Identify strings, integers, floating-point numbers, booleans, and missing values.
Convert text into numbers at an input boundary and handle failed conversion.
Define a conversion's input unit, output unit, and expected behavior.

concepts.title: A variable is a name bound to a value
concepts.text: In Python, amount = 10 binds the name amount to an integer object. Reassigning amount changes which value the name refers to; it does not change all values elsewhere in the program. Use names that describe the role of the value, such as distance_km, rather than an unexplained x. Including units in names prevents a subtle category of bugs: a correct calculation applied to the wrong measurement. Type information and domain meaning are related, but a float alone cannot tell you whether a number means kilometres or dollars.

concepts.title: Representation changes behavior
concepts.text: The string "2" contains a text character. The integer 2 represents a number. Adding two strings joins their text, while adding two integers performs arithmetic. A float represents a number approximately using binary floating-point; many decimal fractions are not represented exactly. For beginner measurement calculations, document a rounding policy. For currency, integer minor units or a carefully chosen Decimal policy are usually clearer than assuming float rounding always matches accounting rules.

concepts.title: Validate at the boundary
concepts.text: User-entered data and API payloads arrive from outside your program. Convert them at a clear boundary before relying on arithmetic. float("2.5") succeeds, while float("two") raises ValueError. Catch the failure when you can return a useful message; do not silently substitute zero. After conversion, check domain rules too: a distance may not be negative, even though -3 is a perfectly valid number. Numeric parsing is therefore only one part of validation.

example.run: Run python converter.py. The standard library is sufficient.
example.context: Convert a text value representing kilometres into metres. The unit appears in both names and output.
example.walkthrough: raw_distance is text because it represents an input boundary. float creates a numeric value for arithmetic. The condition checks a domain rule, not a type rule. Multiplying by 1000 applies the conversion factor. The g format keeps this example's display compact; it does not change the stored numeric value. The except block handles invalid text and rejected negative distances. Try changing raw_distance to an empty string, zero, and -1 and follow the executed path in each case.

exercises.title: Explain two different additions
exercises.task: Run "2" + "2" and 2 + 2. Inspect each operand with type() and explain the difference.
exercises.hint: Do not infer the type from the displayed characters alone.
exercises.check: You can predict 22 versus 4 without running the expressions again.

exercises.title: Reject invalid input
exercises.task: Test empty text, whitespace, two, zero, and a negative distance. Define the desired message for each rejected value.
exercises.hint: Parsing and domain validation are separate decisions.
exercises.check: Rejected input produces a clear message instead of a false conversion result.

exercises.title: Add temperature conversion
exercises.task: Write the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit formula in words, then implement it using a named input and output.
exercises.check: 0 C becomes 32 F and 100 C becomes 212 F.

mistakes: Joining numeric text instead of adding numbers: inspect types at the boundary.
Silently treating invalid input as zero: a fallback value can create a believable but wrong result.
Mixing units or formatting too early: compute using clearly named numeric values, then format for display.
fde: Customer integrations often fail because two systems represent the same idea differently. One export contains numeric text, another uses a different unit, and a third omits missing values. Documenting and validating those boundaries is engineering work. Your converter is a small integration with an explicit contract.

project.title: A reliable unit conversion desk
project.brief: A shop employee needs a small converter for distances and temperatures. Build a program with a clearly selected conversion, labelled inputs and outputs, and helpful handling of invalid input. Keep distance validation separate from temperature rules: negative Celsius values are valid, while the project's distance contract rejects negative distances.
deliverables: A converter supporting kilometres to metres and Celsius to Fahrenheit.
A written input contract for both conversions.
A test-results table with valid, zero, negative, and non-numeric examples.
A short explanation of types and unit names in the implementation.

milestones.title: Define the contract
steps: Write the two formulas and allowed inputs in plain English.
Decide how to display units and how many decimal places are useful.
milestones.check: Your validation rules distinguish distances from temperatures.

milestones.title: Convert and validate
steps: Implement conversion from raw text to a numeric value.
Return a helpful message for invalid text and unsupported conversion names.
milestones.check: A rejected value cannot be mistaken for a successful result.

milestones.title: Prove the boundaries
steps: Run the test matrix and save the results.
Change the input representation deliberately and explain the behavior.
milestones.check: Known reference conversions and invalid-input cases behave as specified.

acceptance: Both conversion formulas produce the documented reference results.
Outputs include the input and output units.
Invalid numeric text produces a useful error message.
Negative temperature and distance inputs follow their separate contracts.
A test-results table records at least four boundary cases.
tests: Helpful validation error and no fabricated result
extensions: Add metres to kilometres and test a round trip within an explicit tolerance.
Add a currency-formatting exercise using integer minor units; keep it separate from live exchange rates.
review: Why does input representation matter to arithmetic?
Which checks are type validation and which are business rules?
Where does rounding happen, and what information can rounding lose?

title: Decisions, repetition, and boundary cases
intro: Conditions let a program choose an action; loops let it repeat an action over data. Together they express business rules such as which ticket needs attention and when processing should stop. Today you will move from isolated if statements to a small ticket-triage workflow with explicit priority rules and a visible summary.
objectives: Trace which branch runs for a given condition, including equality.
Process a collection without skipping or endlessly repeating work.
Translate written priority rules into an ordered decision structure.

concepts.title: Conditions have precise boundaries
concepts.text: The expression count > 10 asks a different question from count >= 10. The first excludes exactly ten; the second includes it. Test the boundary itself and the values on either side. For multiple rules, decide their order: an if/elif chain chooses the first matching branch, whereas separate if statements can run more than one branch. A ticket that is both old and critical must follow a documented priority rule, not whichever order was accidentally typed first.

concepts.title: A loop needs a clear unit of work
concepts.text: A for loop visits items in an iterable. Identify what one iteration means: one ticket, one customer, or one attempt. Keep counters and accumulated results separate from the current item. An empty collection performs zero iterations, so your summary must still be meaningful. Avoid changing the collection you are iterating over unless you understand the behavior; filtering into a new collection is often clearer for a beginner.

concepts.title: Termination belongs in the design
concepts.text: A while loop repeats while its condition is true. If the state used by that condition never changes, the loop can run forever. Interactive programs need a way to exit, and retrying programs need a maximum attempt count or time limit. break stops the loop; continue skips the rest of the current iteration. Neither should hide a missing design decision about what happens to rejected work or unfinished items.

example.run: Run python triage.py or paste the example into the Python lab.
example.context: The critical severity rule takes priority over the age rule. Trace each ticket before running the loop.
example.output:
T1 urgent
T2 review
T3 standard
example.walkthrough: The list contains three dictionaries, each representing one ticket. The for statement binds ticket to each dictionary in turn. For T1, the first condition is true and the other branches are skipped. T2 reaches the age condition and qualifies at exactly 24 hours because the operator includes equality. T3 falls into the else branch. Each iteration assigns priority before it prints, so the previous ticket's result cannot accidentally be reused.

exercises.title: Test the exact boundary
exercises.task: Create tickets aged 23, 24, and 25 hours. Predict their priority.
exercises.hint: Focus on >= rather than the displayed age alone.
exercises.check: Exactly 24 hours follows the written rule.

exercises.title: Count outcomes
exercises.task: Add a counter for urgent tickets and print a summary after the loop.
exercises.hint: Initialise the counter before the loop and increment it only for the matching priority.
exercises.check: The summary is correct for an empty list and for multiple critical tickets.

exercises.title: Bound repeated attempts
exercises.task: Write a three-attempt retry simulation that stops early after success.
exercises.hint: Use a fixed range and break on the successful result.
exercises.check: Failure cannot cause a fourth attempt or an endless loop.

mistakes: Using > where the requirement includes equality: test the threshold explicitly.
Using separate if statements when only one priority should win: write down rule precedence.
Forgetting empty input or stop conditions: the absence of work should still produce a useful summary.
fde: Business policies often contain exceptions and conflicting rules. An FDE asks which rule wins and what happens at the threshold, then records examples before implementing the policy. A short, tested decision table can prevent a long argument after delivery.

project.title: Support-ticket triage queue
project.brief: A support lead needs a repeatable way to review tickets. Build a program that reads a small in-memory ticket list, assigns exactly one priority to each valid ticket, and prints a summary. Critical tickets are urgent; other tickets aged at least 24 hours need review; the rest are standard. Invalid or incomplete tickets must be reported instead of silently classified.
deliverables: A triage program with documented rule precedence.
A sample queue containing normal, critical, old, and invalid tickets.
A summary of each priority and rejected records.
A test table for empty queues and threshold cases.

milestones.title: Write the decision table
steps: Create one example for each rule and one overlapping example.
Agree that critical severity takes precedence over age.
milestones.check: The overlapping example has one unambiguous expected priority.

milestones.title: Process the queue
steps: Use a loop to validate and classify one ticket at a time.
Count outcomes without changing the original queue during iteration.
milestones.check: Every input ticket has a visible result or rejection reason.

milestones.title: Handle edges
steps: Test empty input, missing fields, and 23/24/25-hour boundaries.
Save the queue, output, and rule explanation for review.
milestones.check: Your summary agrees with the individually classified tickets.

acceptance: Each valid ticket receives exactly one documented priority.
Critical severity takes precedence over the age rule.
The 24-hour boundary behaves as specified.
Invalid records and an empty queue are handled visibly.
Priority totals and rejection totals match the processed records.
tests: Urgent only, not both urgent and review
Zero counts and a useful no-work message
Ticket missing severity or with negative age
extensions: Add a maximum batch size and show unprocessed tickets separately.
Make the threshold configurable and test two different policies.
review: What happens when the collection is empty?
Which boundary case was most likely to reveal a bug?

title: Functions, contracts, and useful abstraction
intro: A function gives a small operation a name, explicit inputs, and an observable result. It helps you reason about a program one responsibility at a time. Today you will turn a calculation into a contract and build a quote calculator whose business rules can be tested without reading interactive input or printing a screen.
objectives: Distinguish a function's parameters, return value, and side effects.
Separate pure calculation from input/output code.
Write and test a function contract with normal and invalid inputs.

concepts.title: Name what the operation means
concepts.text: A function should expose a useful idea to its caller. total_cents(price_cents, quantity) tells you more than process(a, b). The caller needs to know allowed inputs, the result, and possible errors. Those expectations are the contract. Implementation details can change while the contract stays stable, letting other parts of the program continue to work. Start with an operation you can describe in one sentence; if the sentence contains several unrelated tasks, the function may be taking on too much.

concepts.title: Return and print are different
concepts.text: return passes a value back to the caller and ends that function call. print writes a representation to an output stream. A function that only prints a total is harder to reuse in a web API or a test. Let calculation functions return values; let the interface decide how to display them. A function with no explicit return returns None in Python. That often explains why a caller unexpectedly receives a missing value after an apparently successful print.

concepts.title: Pure logic is easier to test
concepts.text: A pure calculation uses its inputs to produce a result without modifying external state. It does not read the keyboard, save a file, or call a network service. Such functions are straightforward to test with known examples. Side effects are necessary in real applications, but keep their boundaries visible. The goal is not to create the largest possible number of functions; it is to separate responsibilities where the separation helps you understand and change the system.

example.run: Run python quote.py. The example uses integer cents rather than live currency conversion.
example.context: A line total is calculated in integer minor units. Validation is part of the function contract.
example.code:
def line_total_cents(price_cents, quantity):
    if price_cents < 0 or quantity < 0:
        raise ValueError("Price and quantity must be non-negative")
    return price_cents * quantity

subtotal = line_total_cents(250, 3)
assert subtotal == 750
print(f"Subtotal: {subtotal} cents")
example.walkthrough: def creates a callable function; its body runs when the caller supplies the two arguments. The validation rejects negative inputs before calculating. return gives the integer result to the caller, which stores it as subtotal. The assertion checks a known example independently of the display text. The final print belongs to the interface layer. The example assumes integer inputs; a complete project must document or validate that assumption rather than relying on the function name alone.

exercises.title: Separate output from logic
exercises.task: Replace a calculator that prints inside its calculation with a function that returns its result.
exercises.check: The result can be asserted without capturing printed text.

exercises.title: Test a contract
exercises.task: Check normal quantity, zero quantity, negative quantity, and a non-integer quantity.
exercises.hint: Decide which inputs are supported before writing validation.
exercises.check: Supported values return predictable results and rejected values have clear errors.

exercises.title: Compose operations
exercises.task: Add two line totals and an explicit delivery fee using separate named operations.
exercises.hint: Reuse line_total_cents rather than copying its formula.
exercises.check: Changing one unit price affects only the related line and grand total.

mistakes: Confusing printed output with a return value: inspect what the caller actually receives.
Reading input inside every calculation: isolate the interface so tests can call the logic directly.
Making an abstraction before understanding the rule: a shorter name does not automatically make a clearer contract.
fde: Customer systems change. A useful contract lets you replace a price source, UI, or storage layer without rewriting the business calculation. An FDE explains which changes stay local and which changes affect the contract other teams rely on.

project.title: A reusable quote calculator
project.brief: A small service business creates quotes with line items and a delivery fee. Build calculation functions using integer cents, plus a thin display layer. Define supported prices and quantities explicitly. The first version has no tax integration, discounts, payments, or live exchange rates; those are separate scope decisions.
deliverables: Calculation functions for line totals, subtotal, and grand total.
A readable example quote with two line items.
A written contract for integer prices and quantities.
Tests for zero, negative, and unsupported inputs.

milestones.title: Specify calculations
steps: Write a sample quote and calculate it manually.
Define the unit and valid range of every input.
milestones.check: The manual expected total is available before the code is written.

milestones.title: Build reusable functions
steps: Return calculated values instead of printing inside business functions.
Keep user-facing formatting in a small separate caller.
milestones.check: The same functions can be called from a test or another interface.

milestones.title: Review change impact
steps: Test the boundaries and compare results with the manual quote.
Change the delivery fee and show which function or caller changes.
milestones.check: The change does not alter unrelated line calculations.

acceptance: Calculations use documented integer minor units.
Line, subtotal, and grand-total functions return useful values.
The display layer is separate from the calculation functions.
Zero and invalid inputs follow the written contract.
A manually checked quote and regression examples agree with the implementation.
tests: Zero quantity and a non-zero delivery fee
Zero line total plus the documented fee
Clear rejection rather than a negative quote
Only that line, subtotal, and grand total change
extensions: Introduce a documented percentage-discount policy with explicit rounding.
Use the functions behind a small web form after lesson 13.
review: Which function contracts could another developer rely on?
Why is returning a value different from printing it?
Which possible future change would require a contract change?

title: Collections and data modelling
intro: Real applications usually operate on many records rather than one value. Choosing the shape of those records determines which operations are clear, safe, and efficient enough for the task. Today you will model contacts with stable identifiers, distinguish ordered collections from keyed lookup, and build a contact directory that handles duplicate names deliberately.
objectives: Choose between a list and a dictionary for a specific operation.
Model records with stable IDs rather than ambiguous display names.
Explain mutation, missing keys, and duplicate-record behavior.

concepts.title: Lists preserve a sequence
concepts.text: A list represents an ordered collection. It is useful when display order or visiting each item matters. Indexes describe positions, not permanent identities: removing an earlier item changes later positions. A customer ID therefore should not be inferred from a list index. When you filter a list, decide whether you are producing a new view or deleting records. That distinction becomes important when a UI lets a user search without intending to remove data.

concepts.title: Dictionaries support named lookup
concepts.text: A dictionary associates a key with a value. A stable contact ID can map to a dictionary containing that contact's fields. Looking up a known ID is clearer than searching for a name that may be shared by multiple people. Accessing a missing key with square brackets raises KeyError. get can return a default, but choose a default that preserves meaning: a missing contact is not the same thing as an empty contact record.

concepts.title: A model contains decisions, not just fields
concepts.text: Decide what must be present, what can be missing, and what makes a record unique. Two contacts may share a display name while having different IDs. Updating a contact should preserve its identity. Lists and dictionaries are mutable, so two names can refer to the same object; a change through one reference can be visible through the other. Use an explicit copy when you need an independent record, and understand whether a shallow copy also shares nested objects.

example.run: Run python contacts.py. Records remain in memory in this example; lesson 6 adds persistence.
example.context: Two people share a name, so the program uses IDs for lookup and names only for display.
example.output:
C001 Ali Lahore
C002 Ali Karachi
Contact not found
example.walkthrough: The outer dictionary maps unique IDs to records. Each inner dictionary labels the fields of one contact. items supplies both the identifier and record to each loop iteration. The shared name does not overwrite a record because it is not used as the key. get returns None for the missing ID, which the caller converts into a helpful message. The example's insertion order makes the displayed order predictable, but it is not a substitute for an explicit sort when the product requires alphabetical output.

exercises.title: Search without deleting
exercises.task: Produce a list of contacts whose city matches a query while keeping the original directory unchanged.
exercises.hint: Append matching records to a separate list.
exercises.check: Searching for an unknown city returns no matches without removing contacts.

exercises.title: Update by identity
exercises.task: Change the city of C002 while preserving its ID and the other contact.
exercises.hint: Look up the ID before updating its fields.

exercises.title: Observe shared state
exercises.task: Assign one contact record to another variable, change its city, and inspect the original.
exercises.hint: Assignment does not automatically create a deep copy.
exercises.check: You can explain why the update is visible through both references.

mistakes: Using names as unique keys: duplicate names can overwrite valid people.
Treating a position as a stable ID: positions change when records are inserted or deleted.
Hiding missing records behind empty defaults: an explicit not-found result is easier to diagnose.
fde: A customer data export may contain duplicates, optional fields, and inconsistent identifiers. An FDE asks how records are matched across systems before building an integration. A data model should preserve useful distinctions instead of deleting them to make the code convenient.

project.title: Customer contact directory
project.brief: A small team needs to add, find, update, and list contacts. Build an in-memory directory keyed by stable IDs. Allow duplicate display names, validate required fields, and make a missing ID understandable. Persistence is intentionally left for the next lesson, so today you can concentrate on data shape and operations.
deliverables: A contact model with ID, name, city, and optional email.
Operations to add, look up, update, search, and list records.
A sample dataset containing duplicate names and missing optional values.
An explanation of identity, validation, and ordering decisions.

milestones.title: Model the records
steps: List required and optional fields with sample values.
Choose an ID strategy and document duplicate-name behavior.
milestones.check: Two people with the same name remain separate records.

milestones.title: Implement useful operations
steps: Add lookup and update operations that use the stable ID.
Return search results without mutating the stored directory.
milestones.check: An unknown ID produces an explicit not-found outcome.

milestones.title: Inspect data integrity
steps: Try duplicate IDs, blank names, and missing optional email.
Check that an update preserves all unrelated records.
milestones.check: The dataset still follows the model after all operations.

acceptance: Each contact has a stable unique ID and a non-blank name.
Duplicate display names do not overwrite records.
Lookup and update use IDs and handle missing IDs clearly.
Search does not delete or mutate the original directory.
Required and optional fields are documented and tested.
tests: Two contacts named Ali with different IDs
Rejected or handled by an explicit documented update operation
Blank required name rejected; optional email handled
extensions: Add explicit alphabetical sorting without changing stored identities.
Design an import report that distinguishes accepted, duplicate, and rejected records.
review: Why is an ID different from a display name?
Which operations benefit from keyed lookup?
What did you choose to do with missing and duplicate data?

title: Persistence, errors, and systematic debugging
intro: An in-memory directory disappears when the process stops. A useful tool often needs durable state, but saving state introduces new failure modes: missing files, invalid data, and interrupted writes. Today you will connect persistence to recovery and learn to investigate errors using evidence rather than a sequence of guesses.
objectives: Serialize structured data to JSON and load it back deliberately.
Distinguish missing, corrupt, and invalid stored data.
Read an exception and investigate the relevant failing operation.

concepts.title: Persistence is a boundary
concepts.text: Memory belongs to a running process. A file survives beyond that process, but the file format becomes a contract between versions of the application. JSON represents a useful subset of values such as objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. It does not automatically preserve custom Python objects or validate your business rules. Loading syntactically valid JSON is therefore followed by checking that the stored shape and required fields match what your program expects.

concepts.title: Failures need different recovery policies
concepts.text: A missing data file on first launch can mean an empty directory. A corrupt existing file may represent information the user expects you to preserve. Do not treat both cases as permission to overwrite the file with an empty object. Decide which errors are recoverable, which need user action, and what evidence to keep. For writes, an intermediate file followed by an appropriate replacement can reduce partial-write risks; the exact durability guarantee still depends on the operating system and storage setup.

concepts.title: Debugging starts with reproduction
concepts.text: Read the exception type, message, and relevant stack frames. Identify the input and operation that caused the failure. Reproduce it with the smallest useful example, state a hypothesis, and test one targeted change. Catching every exception and continuing silently removes the evidence you need. A useful error message explains the problem and next action while avoiding private data. After the fix, re-run the successful path as well as the failing case.

example.run: Run python persistence.py. This worked example serializes in memory; the project adds actual file reads and writes.
example.context: JSON parsing and application-level validation are separate checks. A small in-memory example keeps the two concepts visible.
example.output:
Round trip preserved 1 contact
Stored data is not valid JSON; keep the original for investigation
example.walkthrough: dumps converts the dictionary into a JSON text representation, while loads parses that representation into Python values. The isinstance check validates the outer shape and the assertion confirms this sample round trip. A real application must also inspect each contact's fields. The deliberate invalid text produces JSONDecodeError, which is handled specifically. The message recommends preserving the original data instead of pretending a failed read means there are no contacts.

exercises.title: Separate parsing from validation
exercises.task: Load a valid JSON array where the program expects a dictionary. Reject the shape clearly.
exercises.hint: Valid JSON is not necessarily valid application data.
exercises.check: The failure is a schema problem, not incorrectly reported as corrupt JSON.

exercises.title: Record a debugging hypothesis
exercises.task: Introduce a missing contact field and write the input, observed failure, hypothesis, and fix in four short lines.
exercises.hint: Find the operation that assumes the missing field exists.
exercises.check: Your fix addresses the assumption and a regression example remains.

exercises.title: Test recovery locally
exercises.task: Use a temporary project data file to test first launch, a normal save, and a damaged copy.
exercises.hint: Do not experiment on your only copy of useful data.
exercises.check: The normal state reloads and damaged data is not silently overwritten.

mistakes: Equating valid JSON with valid records: validate the expected data shape after parsing.
Returning empty data for every exception: that can hide corruption and cause information loss.
Fixing the symptom without preserving a regression case: keep the input that exposed the assumption.
fde: Customer data is part of the product, not disposable debugging material. An FDE plans how to diagnose a failure, protect existing records, and explain recovery to the operator. A modest contact file is a good place to learn these habits before working with a production database.

project.title: Persistent contact book with recovery
project.brief: Extend the contact directory so records survive closing and reopening the program. Store them in a documented JSON file, validate loaded records, and distinguish first launch from damaged existing data. Add a recovery message and a backup approach that preserves the user's information while you investigate a failure.
deliverables: Save and load operations with a documented data-file path and format.
A validated contact schema compatible with lesson 5.
A recovery policy for missing, malformed, and invalid files.
A restart test and a debugging log for one controlled failure.

milestones.title: Design storage
steps: Choose a data-file location and write a valid sample JSON document.
Define separate behavior for missing data and damaged existing data.
milestones.check: The recovery policy does not erase existing data to hide a failure.

milestones.title: Persist and restore
steps: Save contacts and load them through schema validation.
Close the process, reopen it, and inspect the stored records.
milestones.check: IDs and fields survive a normal restart.

milestones.title: Exercise recovery
steps: Test a damaged copy and record the error path.
Keep a backup and demonstrate recovery without guessing.
milestones.check: A reviewer can follow the recovery steps from your README.

acceptance: Contacts survive a normal process restart.
Loaded data is checked for both JSON syntax and contact shape.
First launch works when the data file is absent.
Corrupt existing data is reported and preserved for recovery.
The README documents the data path, backup, and recovery steps.
tests: An empty usable directory is created according to policy
Both IDs and fields return unchanged
Read malformed JSON from a damaged copy
Useful error; original damaged file preserved
Read valid JSON with an invalid contact shape
Schema error rather than silent acceptance
extensions: Write through a temporary file and explain what guarantee it improves.
Add a format version and a migration plan for a future optional field.
review: How are parsing, validation, and recovery different?
Which failure must not be treated as empty data?
What evidence helped you choose a targeted debugging fix?
